messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Carpenter
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Gustatory (Taste): A specific taste associated with the event, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Avoid Thinking: Thinking about the event
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Marcus

Marcus was thirty-two when the accident happened on a Tuesday afternoon in late September. He had been framing the second story of a residential renovation in Arlington, Virginia—a job he'd bid competitively and was determined to finish ahead of schedule. His crew that day consisted of himself, a newer guy named Derek who was still learning the trade, and Tom, a seasoned carpenter in his sixties who'd worked alongside Marcus for nearly a decade. They were installing headers above a load-bearing wall when Tom stepped backward to check the level of a beam. His boot caught the edge of an open floor joist. In the three seconds it took for him to fall, Marcus watched his body rotate in the air. Tom landed on his left side on the concrete subfloor below—a drop of twelve feet. The sound was not what Marcus expected. It was wet and wrong. When Marcus reached him, Tom's left arm was bent at an angle that made no anatomical sense, and there was blood pooling beneath his head, a metallic taste suddenly present in Marcus's mouth as if he'd bitten his own tongue, though he hadn't.

The emergency response, the hospital waiting room, Tom's wife arriving in shock—all of it became a kind of blur that Marcus could not quite convert into a coherent story. When he tried to explain it to his wife, Keisha, in the days that followed, the words would not come. He could see it all with perfect clarity: the angle of Tom's arm, the blood, the taste. But when he opened his mouth, nothing emerged that felt true. It was as if the event existed only in his body, in the sensations that kept replaying without his permission.

Tom survived, but with a traumatic brain injury and a shattered humerus. He would not return to carpentry. Marcus carried the weight of that knowledge through the winter. By January, six months after the fall, he had developed a pattern he did not fully recognize until Keisha pointed it out: whenever he felt the memory rising—that taste, that image—he would reach for food. Late at night, he would stand in the kitchen and eat an entire box of cereal, or a half-gallon of ice cream, not tasting it, not wanting it, but needing the sensation of fullness, the physical act of swallowing, something to anchor him to the present moment. He gained twenty-three pounds. His clothes no longer fit. He stopped looking at himself in the mirror.

The job sites became increasingly difficult. In March, while installing trim in a new construction, a subcontractor cut his hand on sheet metal. The blood—bright red, vivid—triggered the memory so completely that Marcus lost twenty minutes. He found himself sitting in his truck with no memory of how he'd gotten there, his hands shaking, his body drenched in sweat. He'd been somewhere else entirely. He came to believe that his mind was no longer trustworthy, that it could leave him at any moment without warning. The taste would come unbidden: metallic, copper-tinged, appearing in his mouth when he was eating lunch or kissing Keisha goodnight. When it came, he would dissociate deliberately, trying to leave his body, to blank out the sensation. Sometimes he would succeed; other times he would be stuck between two realities—present but not present, aware of Keisha speaking to him but unable to respond, as if he were behind thick glass.

By summer, Marcus had stopped accepting new contracts. He told clients he was overscheduled. The truth was that he could not trust himself on a job site. He'd watched another carpenter take a fall from a ladder in early June—nothing serious, just a stumble—but the sight of the man's bloodied knee had sent Marcus into a dissociative state that lasted hours. His reputation in the local construction community, built over a decade, began to quietly erode. Keisha, who worked in medical administration, found herself increasingly the sole income earner. They had been saving for a down payment on a house. That plan was now indefinite.

What finally brought Marcus to a therapist's office in late August was not a crisis but an accumulation: the weight gain, the distance that had grown between him and Keisha, the knowledge that he could not return to the work that had defined him. He sat in the intake session, unable to fully articulate why he was there, knowing only that his life had fundamentally broken and that he no longer recognized himself in it. He was terrified that this was permanent—that the man he'd been before Tom's fall was gone forever, and that the person he'd become was someone he could no longer rely on to function.
